profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting is being held at a veterinary academic referral center to evaluate the near-final draft of the CURATIVE Domain 3 evidence-to-recommendation worksheet and summary table for antithrombotic protocols in dogs and cats. The immediate context is that the domain leads must decide whether the current draft is ready to circulate to the wider Delphi panel, with particular attention to how protocol recommendations are phrased for clopidogrel, aspirin, unfractionated heparin, and low-molecular-weight heparins. The agenda is to review whether the protocol table meets the group's intended standard for a 'specific protocol,' whether the supporting evidence language is aligned with the cited literature, whether safety/monitoring notes belong in the protocol table itself, and whether the document is sufficiently complete for Delphi circulation. The expected outcome is a decision to approve the draft with limited edits and send it to the full consensus panel.

members.name: Dr. Leah Moreno
members.role: Veterinary Criticalist and Domain 3 Lead Reviewer
members.expertise: Small-animal emergency and critical care, thrombosis management, evidence synthesis
members.background: Leads the critical care anticoagulation practices committee at a university veterinary hospital and has been coordinating the species-by-drug PICO worksheets for the CURATIVE panel.
members.private_state: She wants the worksheet approved quickly so the Delphi timeline is not delayed, and she is trying to keep the document tightly tethered to what was explicitly reported in the literature rather than turning it into a practice guideline with extra implementation detail.
hidden_assumptions: A 'specific protocol' should only be called supported when the literature points to a single concrete regimen with exact dose, frequency, route, and indication rather than a clinically reasonable range.

When people say the feline clopidogrel evidence supports the protocol, they are mainly referring to the clinical trial evidence in cats at risk of cardiogenic thromboembolism, not laboratory platelet-function studies in healthy cats.
The Domain 3 protocol table is scoped to administration details and high-level cautionary notes, while broader follow-up or laboratory monitoring belongs elsewhere.
A document is 'ready for Delphi' once the recommendation wording, LOE, and study-quality assignments are stable, even if unit harmonization and table polish are finished afterward.

members.name: Dr. Ethan Park
members.role: Veterinary Cardiologist and Evidence Methods Co-Reviewer
members.expertise: Feline cardiomyopathy, arterial thromboembolism prevention, clinical trial interpretation
members.background: Serves at a referral cardiology center and has previously contributed to multicenter reviews of antiplatelet therapy in cats, with a strong interest in translating evidence summaries into usable bedside recommendations.
members.private_state: He wants the final table to be practical enough that panelists and later readers can immediately recognize how they would implement the recommended regimens, especially for feline clopidogrel and heparin products.
hidden_assumptions: A 'specific protocol' can still count as specific if it gives a narrow dosing scheme or default regimen that clinicians can apply, even when the literature supporting it comes from more than one kind of study.
References to the feline clopidogrel protocol naturally pool the randomized clinical trial with platelet-inhibition and pharmacodynamic studies when judging how well the regimen is supported.
If a table is labeled a protocol table, it should include enough practical monitoring language to guide implementation, not just dose, frequency, and route.

A worksheet is not really 'ready to circulate' until the rendered table is close to publication-ready, including harmonized dose units, duration fields, and footnote structure, because panelists will react to the formatting as part of the recommendation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to recommend a 'specific protocol' for selected antithrombotics.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a single regimen tightly anchored to published evidence: exact dose, frequency, route, and clinical context, with little room for interpolation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a clinically usable dosing scheme can count as a specific protocol even if it is expressed as a narrow range, default regimen, or synthesized from several compatible studies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the CURATIVE objective language, so each assumes the other shares the same operational meaning; both are also trying to avoid overclaiming, which makes their agreement sound genuine.

misalignment_points.topic: Which feline clopidogrel evidence they are invoking
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the cat clopidogrel evidence' or 'the feline clopidogrel protocol' as the clearest supported area.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is primarily thinking of the clinical trial evidence in cats with cardiomyopathy or cardiogenic thromboembolism risk that supports the commonly cited 18.75 mg/cat once-daily regimen.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally aggregating that trial with ex vivo platelet inhibition and pharmacodynamic studies in cats, treating the whole cluster as the evidentiary basis for confidence in the regimen.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Clopidogrel is one of the few drugs in this domain that everyone already regards as relatively well supported, so neither feels pressure to name the exact paper set each time they mention it.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the protocol table under monitoring/safety notes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss adding a brief 'monitoring note' or 'safety note' to the protocol table.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means only concise adverse-effect caveats or literature-derived remarks attached to the administration regimen, without expanding into practical laboratory follow-up expectations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this can include implementation-oriented items such as CBC checks, bleeding surveillance, platelet count review, or anti-Xa monitoring prompts where relevant.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they both frame it as a small note rather than a major content block, the scope difference feels like a formatting detail instead of a substantive disagreement about what the table is for.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready to circulate' means before Delphi
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the worksheet should be 'ready for Delphi' or 'ready to circulate' after this review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the core scientific judgments are fixed: recommendation direction, LOE, and quality labels are settled, while presentation-level cleanup can happen after panel feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the document should already be close to final form, with harmonized units, fixed-dose versus mg/kg conventions made consistent, and durations/footnotes standardized before panelists see it.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design review settings, 'ready' often functions as a generic approval phrase, and both assume they are discussing the same threshold because neither sees their standard as controversial.

turns.inner_thought: I need this wrapped today so Domain 3 does not hold up the Delphi schedule. For me, if the recommendation direction, level of evidence, and study-quality calls are stable, then it is ready for Delphi even if the table still needs cosmetic cleanup. I do not want this meeting to drift into making the worksheet publication-ready.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. My main goal today is just to do one last pass on the Domain 3 summary table and decide whether it's ready for Delphi this week.

turns.inner_thought: I mostly want to be sure the recommendations read as usable, especially where we are trying to recommend a specific protocol, and that nobody on the panel gets distracted by avoidable formatting inconsistencies. To me, ready to circulate means close to final in both substance and presentation.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. From my side, I mainly want to confirm that the recommendations read as supported where appropriate and that the draft is clean enough to circulate without confusing panelists.

turns.inner_thought: Clopidogrel in cats is the one place where I think we can truly point to a single evidence-anchored regimen: the clinical trial literature in cats at risk of cardiogenic thromboembolism supports the familiar once-daily fixed dose. Aspirin and most of the heparin products do not rise to that same threshold for a specific protocol; at best we can list dosage schemes reported in the literature.
turns.utterance: If we're looking at where the table is strongest, clopidogrel is still the clearest place where we can recommend a specific protocol, especially on the feline side. Most of the other rows still read more like dosage schemes than evidence-based protocols.

turns.inner_thought: I agree completely on feline clopidogrel. In my mind, that confidence comes from the whole cat clopidogrel evidence package, not just the clinical trial, and that is enough to justify a practical default regimen as a specific protocol. The current wording is probably appropriately strong if we leave it alone.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree with that. The feline clopidogrel protocol is probably the best-supported line in the table, and the wording that's there now feels appropriately strong given the cat clopidogrel evidence already summarized in the worksheet.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep the protocol table tightly scoped. Domain 3 should not become a bedside management document. The table should stay focused on administration details and maybe a short caution if the literature explicitly mentions bleeding or similar concerns; follow-up testing and broader monitoring belong elsewhere if anywhere.
turns.utterance: On aspirin and the heparin rows, I'd favor keeping the table focused on dose, frequency, and route, and then maybe a very short safety note where needed. I just don't want the protocol section to sprawl beyond what Domain 3 is trying to do.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that as keeping it concise, not as excluding implementation prompts. If the table is a protocol table, a brief monitoring note should still include practical follow-up like watching for bleeding, checking CBCs, and flagging anti-Xa where relevant. Otherwise readers will have a regimen without enough guidance to use it.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I do think a brief monitoring note could help, though—just enough to cue practical follow-up, like bleeding checks and a few relevant review points where they matter, so the protocol table is easier to use.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we have the recommendation wording, LOE, and quality assessments locked, I am comfortable moving forward. Harmonizing units and cleaning up footnotes can happen after panel review; those are polish items, not reasons to delay circulation.
turns.utterance: For me, once the LOE and quality tags are locked, I'd consider the worksheet ready for Delphi. I'd be comfortable letting unit harmonization and some footnote polishing happen on the next pass.

turns.inner_thought: I'm almost aligned, but I really do not think it is ready to circulate until the rendering looks coherent. The fixed-dose feline clopidogrel line next to mg/kg anticoagulants, and the inconsistent duration wording, are exactly the kinds of things panelists react to. Also, if we are recommending a specific protocol, presentation consistency matters because it signals whether the scheme is genuinely ready for use.
turns.utterance: I'm almost there too, but I'd really like the dosage schemes standardized before circulation, especially how the fixed-dose feline clopidogrel entry sits beside the mg/kg anticoagulant rows, and also the duration wording in the footnotes. That would make it feel more ready to circulate to me.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with limited cleanup, but I want to preserve the scientific boundaries. Clopidogrel stays the strongest supported protocol because of the feline clinical trial context; aspirin in cats should clearly not read as suitable sole therapy; and any note we add should stay concise and tied to what the papers actually reported, not expand into broader monitoring instructions.
turns.utterance: I think the way to land this is: keep clopidogrel as the strongest supported protocol, leave aspirin in cats as not suitable as sole therapy, and add only concise notes where the literature explicitly gives safety context. If we do that and clean the presentation a bit, I think we're in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: That's acceptable if the final pass includes the practical formatting and note structure I care about. I'll sign off once those edits are in. I still see this as needing to look near-final before the wider panel sees it, because they'll respond to the table as a protocol document, not just a worksheet.
turns.utterance: That works for me. Once those final edits are incorporated, I'll sign off, and I think the panel will move through it smoothly if the table goes out looking like a near-final protocol document.
